title: A lifelong reading
hook: a plan to read the whole Qur'an regularly for life
tomorrow: which line is called the master of all asking forgiveness?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Juz' 'Amma: the short surahs, heard again, and the old argument between carrying the words and opening them. The first part you knew. Today the whole passages end, with the whole book.
screen: `THE FIRST PART YOU KNEW.` → `THE WHOLE BOOK.`

segments.voice: A favorite hoodie gets softer every year you wear it. A paperback you've reread goes soft at the corners and falls open to your page by itself. Some families keep a Qur'an like that: the spine creased, a ribbon in it, the corner of a page darkened by one thumb. It has weight in the hand. It smells like a shelf in a particular house. And it raises a real question at the end of these passages. After reading it in pieces, how does someone read the whole book, again and again, for life?
screen: `SOFT AT THE CORNERS.` → `A RIBBON, A CREASED SPINE.` → `HOW DO YOU READ IT FOR LIFE?`

segments.voice: Sahih al-Bukhari has a story about exactly that. A young companion, Abdullah ibn Amr, had decided to read the whole Qur'an every night. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ heard, and told him: read it through in a month. Abdullah said he had the strength for more. The Prophet came down with him, step by step, and stopped at seven nights: no faster than that. Here's the part to tell a friend tonight. Years later, grown old and weaker, Abdullah wished he had taken the easier pace he'd been offered. A young man's sprint, and an old man's wish. Another hadith in the same collection, from Aisha, says the deeds most beloved to Allah are the ones done regularly, even if they're small. So the plan the tradition hands down isn't a race. It's a portion. Some call it a wird: a daily share, a page, a part of a part, whatever you can keep, with the ribbon moved forward each day. Hold the book and feel it. The weight in your hand is the whole of it. The ribbon is today. The point isn't finishing once and putting it on a shelf. It's coming back to the same pages at twenty, at forty, at seventy, and finding they've grown with you. The book, for life.
screen: `THE WHOLE BOOK, EVERY NIGHT?` · `A MONTH. NO FASTER THAN SEVEN.` · `AN OLD MAN'S WISH.` · `SMALL, AND KEPT.` · then, large: `THE BOOK, FOR LIFE.`

segments.voice: Pick up a book near you: the Qur'an if you have one, or any book you mean to keep reading. Feel its weight, open it, and run a finger down one page. Then choose today's portion, small enough that you could keep it tomorrow too, and mark the place with whatever is at hand: a ribbon, a receipt, a leaf.
screen: `FEEL THE WEIGHT.` · `ONE PAGE UNDER A FINGER.` · `MARK THE PLACE.`

segments.voice: A lifelong reading: the whole book, read in portions and kept up for years, at a pace the Prophet ﷺ set himself: steady, not frantic.
The line for today: the book, for life, since a portion you can keep beats a finish you can't. Whole passages, complete.

screen: `DAY 1600 COUNTS.` → `WHOLE PASSAGES · 24 OF 24.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT'S THE MASTER OF ASKING FORGIVENESS?`

howItsDone: Some Muslims keep a daily portion of the Qur'an (a wird) and read the whole book through over a month or longer, again and again; printed copies are divided into parts to make a daily portion easy to find.

notes: Abdullah ibn Amr's story: reading every night, told 'in a month', then down to seven (Bukhari 5054); his wish in old age that he had accepted the concession (Bukhari 5052, also 1975 for fasting). Confirm the numbers and that the 'wish' is in 5052.
Aisha's hadith: 'the most beloved deeds to Allah are the most regular, even if few' (Bukhari 6464). The gloss says Aisha 'passed on his sayings'.
